items.paragraph: For decades, government has used Artificial Intelligence (AI) to perform specialised and general tasks, such as:
investigating patterns of fraud
providing information through virtual assistants
digitising and organising physical documents.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Recent advances, including generative AI create new opportunities and challenges. Governments must build and maintain public trust to embrace these opportunities.

lessons.title: Why does this matter to you?

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: The community expects government to be an exemplar of the responsible use of AI.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
We need to meet this expectation when we choose to use AI in our work. 

This training will give you a basic understanding of AI and how to use it responsibly. By completing this course, you will be:
informed on the applications and risks of AI
capable of applying relevant advice
confident about when it's suitable to use generative AI
empowered to apply your own judgement with AI.

items.title: Next: What is AI?
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a field of technologies used to make predictions or perform tasks that would normally require a person.
AI usually overlaps enough with human intelligence to be useful, even though they learn and work in different ways. These are some common terms you might have heard before.

items.title: Machine learning
items.description: Techniques and technology which allow computer networks to find and learn from patterns in data. It has a significant role in most AI fields.

items.title: AI models
items.description: A computer program that was trained on patterns in data so it can make predictions or perform tasks.

items.title: Computer vision
items.description: Techniques to identify patterns and make predictions about real-world objects as seen through images and video.

items.title: Natural language processing
items.description: Techniques to process, interpret and respond to written or spoken human language.

items.title: Generative AI
items.description: A type of machine learning that can generate new and convincing text, images or sounds from conversational prompts.

items.title: Training data
items.description: The starting data which an AI model learns prediction capabilities from. Flawed or unrepresentative training data may embed biases into the model.

items.title: Next: Where is AI used?
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: AI has existed for decades in specialised software and behind the scenes of popular platforms.

items.heading: Recent advances, including generative AI, offer new ways to interact with AI and use it across many scenarios.
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Here’s some examples of where you might encounter AI in everyday life.

items.title: Search engines
items.description: AI-powered algorithms decide the rank of web pages and personalise results based on your search and browsing history. Social media feeds also use AI in a similar way.

items.title: Voice assistants
items.description: Intelligent assistants, like Siri or Alexa, process your voice commands, recognise keywords and decide the best action to take in response.

items.title: Generative AI chatbots
items.description: Generative AI takes conversational instructions or questions to create replies or complete tasks in general-use tools, like ChatGPT or Copilot, and an increasing number of customer service chatbots with a narrow scope or purpose.

items.title: Document scanning
items.description: Whether it’s on your phone or in a digital service, AI is used to scan physical documents, recognise handwritten or printed text and use the results to organise information.

items.title: Data analytics
items.description: Data analysis tools use AI to identify, sort or classify large volumes of information, in a way that’s faster than humans could but easy for us to verify its accuracy.

items.title: Maps and directions
items.description: Online navigation services will calculate the best route from A to B, using a mountain of information from simple distances to your past journeys and real-time traffic.

items.title: Autocomplete
items.description: Your smartphone suggests corrections, emojis or even a quick reply based on your past typing habits.

items.feedback: All of these options are great examples! AI powers many features of the tools and software we use every day, even though it might not be obvious to us.

items.title: Next: AI and generative AI
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Many types of AI have been used in technology, companies and governments for years.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Recently, generative AI has introduced more people than ever with to a hands-on way to use AI. We can interact with it through natural conversation and it can generate convincing text, images or sounds in response.
This creates new opportunities and risks for government, which is why some of this training focuses on generative AI specifically.
You might encounter generative AI within everyday tools and technology, but it may not always be as obvious as a chatbot.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: You might use it in software that lets you:
type a conversational instruction instead of picking settings and options
press a button to generate unique text or images.

items.title: Next: How generative AI works
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: It's easier to make responsible choices once you know the basics of how generative AI works.

items.heading: How generative AI is trained

items.paragraph:
Generative AI is ‘trained’ on large amounts of text, images, sounds or other information. It breaks this data into small pieces to find and learn from common patterns.

Developers can ‘fine tune’ to prioritise certain patterns, but the quality and quantity of training data has the biggest impact on its predictions and outputs.

Facts, meaning or ideas don't mean the same thing to generative AI as they do to us, so it might produce the wrong information.

Usually, the first step to using generative AI is an instruction or question, also called a 'prompt'.

It draws from its training to predict, one by one, the words most likely to follow the prompt. Some generative AI models can do this with images, sounds and video.

This is how generative AI creates an ‘output’ of convincing text, images or sounds, even if it’s factually untrue.

items.heading: Why generative AI isn't always accurate
items.paragraph: When we show up to the present moment with all of our senses, we invite the world to fill us with joy. The pains of the past are behind us. The future has yet to unfold. But the now is full of beauty simply waiting for our attention.

Generative AI makes predictions with a touch of randomness – also called ‘temperature’ – to generate conversational outputs.

This means it will never produce the same output twice and might generate convincing statements that are misleading or factually untrue.

You can offset this by providing clear prompts, specific instructions and relevant supporting information, but you should always check outputs for relevance, biases and accuracy.

items.title: Next: Safe, responsible use
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: The community expects government to be an exemplar of the responsible use of AI.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph:
People who work in government should have the confidence and support to make responsible choices about using AI.

Many resources about existing technology also apply to AI, like your agency's ICT use policies, values and code of conduct. But some decisions will not have an easy or clear direction.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: AI Ethics frameworks such as Australia's AI Ethics Principles, can guide your choices about using AI to:
benefit individuals, society and the environment and ensure its not inaccurate or misleading
respect human rights, diversity and the autonomy of individuals
be inclusive and accessible, and ensure it does not involve or result in unfair discrimination against individuals, communities or groups
uphold privacy rights, data protection and data security laws.

items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.title: Drag each principle to the action you should take to uphold it.

answers.title: Accountability
answers.matchTitle: You should be able to explain, justify and take ownership of your advice and decisions.

answers.title: Transparency and explainability
answers.matchTitle: You should be transparent about where and how you use AI in your work.

answers.title: Human-centred values
answers.matchTitle: Only use outputs that respect human rights, diversity and the autonomy of individuals.

answers.title: Contestability
answers.matchTitle: Identify how people can challenge the use of AI or its outcomes in your work.

answers.title: Reliability and safety
answers.matchTitle: Only use AI when it reliably performs its intended purpose.

answers.title: Fairness
answers.matchTitle: Make sure outputs are fair and meet community expectations before using them.

answers.title: Human, societal and environmental wellbeing
answers.matchTitle: Consider how using AI will benefit individuals, society and the environment.

answers.title: Privacy protection and security
answers.matchTitle: Only use AI in a way that meets your data privacy, protection and security obligations.

items.feedback: Australia’s eight AI Ethics Principles are designed to ensure AI is safe, secure and reliable.

items.title: Next: You remain accountable
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: We’re individually accountable for how we use AI and its outputs in our work.

items.heading: To remain accountable for your use of AI, you must:
items.paragraph: To remain accountable for your use of AI, you must:
explain, justify and own your advice and decisions
assume prompts and supporting information could become public
ensure personal, classified or sensitive information isn’t inappropriately used or revealed.

items.heading: Apply the golden rules whenever you evaluate how to use AI in your work, such as when you’re deciding:

items.paragraph: if AI is appropriate for a task
if it's the most effective tool for the task
what to use in your prompts
how to use the resulting outputs.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: The next section explores these milestones and how to put AI to work by making responsible, effective choices.

items.title: Next: Putting AI to work
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.title: Before you use AI
items.description: Before you even begin to use AI at work, ask yourself a few easy questions.
If there’s not an easy or clear direction, use AI ethics frameworks such as Australia’s AI Ethics Principles to guide your choices in a safe, responsible way.

items.title: What am I trying to achieve?
items.description:
Keep the requirements and ideal outcome of your task in mind to decide which:

  • tools to use
  • stakeholders to involve
  • processes to follow.

items.title: Would it be appropriate to use AI?
items.description:
Some general-use tools, like generative AI, hold unique risks in policy and service delivery.

Alongside AI ethics frameworks, consider how you will manage prompts and outputs for:

  • accuracy – how will you verify that information is accurate and relevant?

  • bias – how will you identify and counter biases in prompts and outputs?

  • sensitivity – how will you prevent, identify or remediate the use of personal, classified, sensitive or copyright-protected information?

  • transparency – how will you make it clear where AI has influenced your advice or decisions, and allow them to be contested?

items.title: What do I need to know before starting?
items.description:
Not every choice will be easy to decide, so familiarise yourself with:

  • your agency’s own AI and ICT use policies

  • whole-of-government guidance, such as the Australian Government's Guidance for using generative AI

  • your workplaces' values, code of conduct and other requirements.

items.title: Test your knowledge
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.title: We should consider biases when using AI to:

answers.title: prevent biases or negative assumptions in our work

items.title: It’s important to maintain transparency when using AI because:

answers.title: people should understand how it was trained and makes predictions

items.title: We need to consider personal, classified, sensitive or copyright-protected information to:

answers.title: evaluate when the benefits of AI outweigh privacy or security risks
anonymise prompts and supporting information before using them
meet the obligations, policies and expectations of government staff

items.title: We should make sure prompts and AI outputs are accurate:

answers.title: to test our own understanding of the subject matter
because it doesn’t understand facts, ideas or meaning the same as us
so people don’t have a reason to contest government using it

lessons.title: Deciding if it's right for you

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: AI is only helpful if it’s helpful to you.

Some AI tools, including generative AI, might help you complete general tasks faster so you can focus on what you do best. Whether you’ve used AI already or not, here are some ways to explore if it’s the right tool for the job.

items.title: Tasks with plenty of background information
items.description: AI performs well with lots of information, like generating a summary of a long document or listing action items from a meeting transcript.

items.title: Brainstorming, rephrasing and other general tasks
items.description: AI perform well on tasks that are general in nature, like brainstorming the structure of an email, setting up a document template or trying different ways to phrase a sentence.

items.title: Tasks that take a long time but are easy to verify
items.description:
AI can be useful on simple, repeatable tasks with outputs that are easy to validate.

Try using it to find names and descriptions scattered throughout documents, assign categories to a group of files or images, or search the internet to find helpful starting points for further research on a subject.

items.paragraph: You don't always have to use AI

Just because you have access to an AI tool doesn’t mean you have to use it.

You might have specialist skills or non-AI tools to complete tasks faster, more reliably or to a higher quality. It might not be suitable for the task if you spend more time:

  • correcting for inaccurate, biased or sensitive information

  • editing or adjusting to meet the desired content style

  • verifying and removing unreliable citations or supporting information

  • making changes to work that uses AI based on manager feedback.

items.title: Being accountable for your use of AI

slides.title: Your agency held a survey to inform its next corporate plan.
slides.description: You’ve been asked to provide a quick summary of the findings and are considering using a generative AI assistant to help you.

responses.feedback: Not quite. You can use AI tools if they are suitable for the task and can meet your needs.
responses.description: Don’t use a generative AI tool to summarise lots of data.

responses.feedback: Not quite. While an AI tool could help you, remain accountable by evaluating if it would be appropriate to use and is the best tool for the task.
responses.description: Use the AI tool and report key findings to your manager.

responses.feedback: Correct! You can use generative AI and critically analyse its outputs, then report key findings to your manager with the disclaimer that AI was used.

slides.title: You can use AI tools if they are suitable for the task and meet your needs.
slides.description: While using an AI tool can be helpful, there are essential steps you must take to ensure you are accountable. Being accountable means you've taken the right steps to support your use of AI tools.

items.title: Next: Using prompts and information
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: From training to prompting, what you get out of an AI tool is only as good as what goes in.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: Consciously consider the quality and integrity of your prompts and supporting information, such as documents or datasets, which you input into AI tools.

items.title: Prompt with quality
items.description:
Take the time to ensure you provide an AI tool with:

  • simple, clear and specific prompts
  • essential or relevant supporting information
  • robust, complete and up-to-date files or datasets.

items.title: Prompt with integrity
items.description:
Work with colleagues and subject matter experts to:

  • counter biases and assumptions in your own prompts and the data you use
  • prevent personal, classified, sensitive or copyright-protected information being revealed
  • ensure your prompt and supporting information is fair, accurate and relevant.

items.title: Next: Using outputs
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: We must be able to explain, justify and take ownership of our advice and decisions and consider the risks of using AI.
With that in mind, consider how will you review, identify and adjust AI outputs for:

Accuracy

Is it verifiably accurate and relevant?

Bias

Is it fair and free of implicit bias or
negative assumptions?

Sensitivity

Does it reveal private, classified, sensitive or copyright-protected information?

Transparency

Is it clear where the output is used and how to contest it?

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: When an AI tool has broad uses, its risks will be similarly broad and general, making them a bit harder to predict. Some simple choices can help you catch or prevent them outright.
Use AI for early ideation or drafts, not a final pass.
Plan adequate time to review and consult on work that uses AI outputs.
Ensure humans make, can explain and own key and final decisions.

items.title: Deciding when to use generative AI

slides.title: You need to write a report about leadership in organisations.
slides.description: This will be informed by publicly available research on the gender identity of people in senior positions. You have access to a generative AI tool which you think could help you write it.

responses.feedback: Not quite! It’s great to be cautious but, as long as you’re alert to the risk of inaccuracies and the risk of gender and other biases, you can make responsible choices with generative AI.
responses.description: Don’t use the generative AI tool because it will generate outputs with biases and assumptions.

responses.feedback: Correct! It can be useful for an early draft and publicly available information is trustworthy and safe to use. Take the time to review the draft for biases and inaccuracies before using it.
responses.description: Consider using the tool to generate an early draft, making use of the publicly available research.

responses.feedback: Not quite! Generative AI doesn't understand facts and ideas the way we do. Instead, use clear, specific prompts for an early draft and review it for biases and inaccuracies before you use it.
responses.description: Use the tool to write the entire report, as it normally generates pretty accurate outputs and was trained on lots of data to begin with.

slides.title: Generative AI is a useful tool for generating early drafts.
slides.description: However, if we fail to identify and mitigate biases or inaccuracies in prompts and outputs, it could have an unfair or dangerous impact on people, and marginalised or underrepresented groups.

items.paragraph: Before you use outputs in government work, always take the time to:
Consider how AI might inadvertently create biased or unfair outcomes.
Consider if you have the right skills and knowledge, or access to people and resources, to help you identify and mitigate biases and errors in your prompts and outputs

Recognise where you may need to consult experts or people with lived experience, such as gender and sexual diversity, gender identity and expression multicultural communities, First Nations peoples, people living with disability and people facing different social or economic circumstances.

items.title: Final step: Where to find advice
items.completeHint: Complete the content above before moving on.

items.paragraph: It's okay if you need a refresh down the track.

items.heading: Heading
items.paragraph: There's one easy thing to remember: if you're about to use AI start by checking advice from your agency and government.

items.heading: Follow your agency's advice first
items.paragraph: Government agencies and their staff are ultimately responsible for how they adopt AI. Always follow your agency’s advice and policies. Ask for help from the relevant internal teams if you need it.

items.heading: Check in with whole-of-government advice
items.paragraph:
Your agency has to align with the whole-of-government approach to AI, so you can always check in with: 

  • whole-of-government guidance, such as the Australian Government's Guidance for using generative AI

  • government expectations such as Australia’s Public Service Values and Code of Conduct

  • AI ethics frameworks such as Australia’s AI Ethics Principles. 

To quickly find many of these resources in the Australia context, visit digital.gov.au/ai/resources.

description:
This training module will provide you with a foundational knowledge of AI, the principles of safe and responsible use, and how to put these to work as government staff.

This training module was developed for and by the Australian Government to support the implementation of the Policy for the responsible use of AI in government. The module therefore refers to Australian specific resources that may not be applicable to your jurisdiction.
